correctness.rationale: For each set W of omitted originals, all edge-vertices internal to W are forced. These dominate every nonisolated vertex of G[W]; each remaining vertex v in W needs a nonempty selection from its incident star. Such stars are mutually disjoint and disjoint from internal edges. All other edge-vertices have a selected old endpoint and are free. The fixed-W generating product follows, including zero terms for omitted degree-zero originals. Its least feasible degree is n-|W|+e_W+|I_W|. The savings from n are the sum of |V|-|E| over nontrivial components, at most one per component. Edges taken one per component give an induced matching in G, and omitting the endpoints of a maximum induced matching attains the bound. Equality forces a tree in every nontrivial component and exactly the specified boundary choice at each isolate, with no selections in the free class; W is recovered from its dominating set, so the multiplicity formula does not overcount. The complete/biclique specializations follow by listing their eligible induced trees; the biclique star count subtracts its twice-counted single edges. The edgeless case forces all originals, including the empty set of a null graph. Independent replay on 79 graphs (all labeled roots through four vertices and additional complete, biclique and disconnected cases) checked 47,735 candidate subsets, full coefficients and the complete list of minimum sets against direct adjacency enumeration. residual_risks: The finite checks are corroboration only. The all-graph proof is for a single subdivision of every edge of a simple undirected root, not repeated subdivisions or multigraphs.

evidence: The earlier independent-domination theorem gives i(S(G))=|V|-im(G). If an ordinary dominating set selects s_uv adjacent to a selected original, delete s_uv when both endpoints are selected, or replace s_uv by the other endpoint otherwise. Domination persists because the only neighbors of s_uv are its two endpoints, and s_uv itself remains dominated. The number of selected subdivision vertices decreases; iteration gives an independent dominating set of no larger size.
Consequently gamma=i on the subdivision graph, and the general scalar identity is already implied even though the prior invariant has a different name.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Independent and ordinary domination are different set enumerators even when their minima have the same size. An ordinary minimum in S(P4), for original P4=1–2–3–4, is {3,s_12,s_34}; 3 is adjacent to s_34, and omitted original 4 is isolated in G[W]. This minimum cannot be counted by the independent enumerator.

value.rationale: The product formula expresses a standard graph invariant directly in root-graph data and explains precisely which boundary choices create nonindependent minima. It reduces the enumerative description from subsets of original and subdividing vertices to subsets of the originals and produces the entire minimum family, not just an optimum value recoverable from known work. That structural enumeration applies uniformly to all finite simple roots, including isolates and disconnected graphs.
residual_risks: No unrestricted polynomial-time computation, nor new value for a known isolated scalar case, is claimed.
